Newborn babies know very little about the world into which they have just been born. Here, they are immersed in sensations: sounds, touch, movement, smells, tastes and (more dimly at first) sights. From this flood of information, they must work out which patterns matter, which recur, and which can be recognised again. This learning begins early, and everything a child later understands and says is built on it.

This section traces that learning in two passes. It first follows word learning as it unfolds in typical development: how infants find word forms in the speech they hear, attach meanings to them, remember them, and eventually say them. It then revisits each step for children with Down syndrome, asking where the machinery runs differently and where it does not, asks what vocabulary is for in the wider language a child goes on to build, and draws out what this implies for teaching -- and why accurately described vocabulary trajectories, the subject of the rest of this report, matter for practice.

## Early sensations

Babies begin to experience some sensations from before birth. Hearing is functional from around 24 to 28 weeks of gestation, although the fetus only receives muffled sounds -- rhythm, stress and intonation rather than discernible consonants and vowels. Nonetheless, this is sufficient for newborns to already prefer their mother's voice over another woman's and distinguish their native language from unfamiliar ones [@gerhardtFetalExposuresSound2000; @gervainSpeechPerceptionLanguage2010].

Vision is less well developed at birth. Acuity (sharpness of perception) at birth is limited, and so a newborn has to be roughly twenty times closer than an adult to make out the same detail. Contrast sensitivity is also poor. Yet, newborns soon orient towards face-like patterns and recognise their mother's face [@simionFacePerceptionProcessing2015].

Touch, taste, smell and the sense of movement and body position are all comparatively mature at birth, as is the sense of hunger, temperature, and internal discomfort. Much of a newborn's earliest learning concerns their own body, its states, and the effects their actions have on the people around them.

## Learning what to ignore

From birth, infants can hear sound patterns in speech that their native language does not use. From around 6 months, they begin to lose this ability as speech perception becomes tuned to the language they hear around them [@gervainSpeechPerceptionLanguage2010; @kuhlEarlyLanguageAcquisition2004]. This narrowing is a feature, not a fault: tuning to the distinctions the native language actually uses is what lets its words be recognised quickly and reliably. Learning a language is partly learning what to ignore.

## Putting the senses together

Some properties of the world are available to more than one sense at once: rhythm, tempo, duration, intensity, and synchrony. When a sound and a sight change together in time, they are probably coming from the same event. By about 4 months, infants look longer at a face whose mouth movements match a vowel they are hearing [@kuhlBimodalPerceptionSpeech1982]. This is the beginning of the machinery that will eventually bind a sound to a thing.

Categorisation begins well before naming. By 3 to 4 months infants distinguish cats from dogs [@quinnEvidenceRepresentationsPerceptually1993] and sort simple event types such as one object being contained in, or supported by, another [@baillargeonInfantsPhysicalWorld2004]. Infants are building a structured world some months before they have any words for it. Some accounts hold that a good deal of this structure is present from the start; others that it is constructed gradually from experience. The evidence does not settle the question, and the defensible position is that infants clearly do more than a blank-slate account predicts and probably less than the strongest nativist accounts claim.

## Finding the words

Written language has spaces. Spoken language does not. Infants must work out where one spoken word stops and where the next word begins in a continuous stream of sound.

Familiar word forms, such as the baby's own name, are recognised by about 4.5 months [@mandelInfantsRecognitionSound1995]. By 7.5 months infants can extract a repeated form from fluent speech and recognise it later [@jusczykInfantsDetectionSound1995]. Several cues contribute: the transitional probability between syllables (within a word, one syllable predicts the next more reliably than across a word boundary) [@saffranStatisticalLearning8MonthOld1996], the stress pattern of the language, prosodic boundaries (the pauses and pitch movements that mark off phrases), and which sound sequences are legal in the language at all. Frequently occurring words appear to act as anchors, though they may need to reach a threshold of familiarity before they help [@frostExploringAnchorWord2020].

How well an infant does this predicts vocabulary later. In a longitudinal study of infants tested at 17 months and followed to 30 months, segmentation performance was related to both receptive and expressive vocabulary size concurrently and over time -- but *not* to the rate of vocabulary growth [@frostNonadjacentDependencyLearning2020]. That distinction -- level versus rate -- is easy to skate over and worth holding onto: the finding concerns where a child is, not how fast they are moving.

### Hearing in Down syndrome {#sec-ds-hearing}

For children with Down syndrome, this stage of learning often runs on a degraded signal. Otitis media with effusion -- persistent fluid in the middle ear -- is extremely common. In a prospective Glasgow cohort of 79 preschool children followed through an annual surveillance clinic, prevalence was 93% at age 1, falling to 68% by age 5; no child in that cohort had significant sensorineural impairment, the kind arising in the inner ear or auditory nerve [@barrPrevalenceEarNose2011]. A Belgian cross-sectional series of 107 children also found prevalence highest at age 1, at 67%, and reported that children with fluid in both ears had median hearing thresholds around 37 dB, compared with 28 dB for those with at least one normally ventilated ear [@marisCrosssectionalAnalysisOtitis2014]; a larger Egyptian series likewise found hearing loss in about half of 170 children, almost all of it conductive -- arising in the middle ear rather than the inner ear -- and mostly mild and bilateral [@yahiaPrevalenceHearingImpairment2025]. A loss of that size is described as mild, and it is easy to miss, but it sits precisely in the range that blurs the quiet, high-frequency parts of speech.

The practical implication is not subtle. During the period when infants are doing their most intensive work on the sound structure of their language, a large proportion of children with Down syndrome are doing it through a degraded signal, and the degradation fluctuates from week to week. Regular hearing surveillance is not a routine formality; it protects the input on which everything downstream depends.

## Learning what words mean

Finding word forms is not the same as knowing what they mean. A word is usually heard amid many possible meanings: when someone says "rabbit", the animal, its ears, its hopping and the hutch are all in view at once. No single moment can settle what a new word picks out. Children resolve the ambiguity across many moments -- meanings that recur alongside a word survive, guesses that fail are replaced -- so it is repeated encounters in varied contexts, not any single teaching moment, that do the work [@trueswellProposeVerifyFast2013; @kachergisWordLearningAssociations2018]. How completely the mechanisms demonstrated in laboratories scale up to the noise and ambiguity of everyday life is still debated [@smithUnrealizedPromiseInfant2014].

Understanding runs well ahead of speech, and begins earlier than was long assumed. By 6 to 9 months -- months before their first spoken words -- infants look towards the right object when they hear common nouns for foods and body parts [@bergelson69MonthsHuman2012], and this early word knowledge is already organised: infants confuse related meanings with one another more than unrelated ones [@bergelsonNatureOriginsLexicon2017]. Comprehension then strengthens markedly soon after the first birthday. The speech infants hear changes rather little across this period; what changes is the learner, as maturing attention, memory and social understanding let the same input teach more [@bergelsonComprehensionBoostEarly2020].

Recordings of everyday life from the infant's own point of view show what a good word-learning moment looks like. Toddlers learn an object's name most reliably in moments when that object is close, large and centred in their view -- usually because they are holding it [@pereiraBottomupViewToddler2014]. A small set of pervasive objects dominates infants' visual experience of mealtimes and play, and these objects disproportionately supply the first nouns [@clerkinRealworldVisualStatistics2017]. Naming works best when it meets attention that is already engaged: infants' sustained attention to objects during play -- supported by parents who name the object at the right moment -- predicts vocabulary months later [@yuInfantSustainedAttention2019], and infants who follow gaze and point earn more of these moments [@brooksInfantGazeFollowing2008].

## Remembering words

A word encountered once can be linked quickly to a likely meaning. Young children do this readily -- it is known as "fast mapping" -- but a quick link is not yet durable knowledge. Robust word knowledge is built up over repeated encounters and consolidated between them, in part during sleep, as new words become integrated with the words a child already knows [@davisComplementarySystemsAccount2009].

Learning a word also means learning its sound pattern, precisely enough to recognise it in fluent speech and eventually to say it. Two memory systems contribute. Verbal short-term memory -- holding a brief sequence of sounds in mind -- has long been linked to vocabulary acquisition, so closely that it has been described as a language learning device [@baddeleyPhonologicalLoopLanguage1998]. Alongside it operates a slower, cumulative route: sound sequences that recur across occasions are gradually learned long term, an ability that is partly separable from short-term capacity [@pageModelLinkingImmediate2009]. The distinction matters for this report, because in Down syndrome the two routes come apart.

## Saying words

Saying a word demands more than understanding one. The child must retrieve the word's sound pattern, plan the movements of tongue, lips, jaw and breath that produce it, and execute them clearly enough to be understood -- among the most intricate motor skills humans ever learn. Production therefore lags comprehension in every child. In typical development, about 80% of children say at least one word by 12 months, and more than 90% say at least seven words by 18 months [@frankWordbankOpenRepository2017].

## Gathering pace

Once production begins, it accelerates: from a handful of words at 12 months, many typically developing children reach several hundred by 24 months, with word learning speeding up conspicuously between 18 and 24 months. This acceleration is often called a "vocabulary spurt", but it need not reflect any sudden change in the child. When many words are being learned in parallel and words vary in difficulty, steady learning produces exactly this curve: the easiest words are learned first, and the child's accumulating skill brings progressively larger bands of words within reach [@mcmurrayDefusingChildhoodVocabulary2007]. What the curve reflects is continuous growth in the underlying system, not a switch being flipped.

Around that average curve, typically developing children vary enormously -- one of the best-documented facts about early vocabulary [@fensonVariabilityEarlyCommunicative1994; @frankWordbankOpenRepository2017]. Two children of the same age can differ by hundreds of words with both developing typically. A single measurement also conflates two different facts: where a child is, and how fast they are moving. Trajectories fitted to repeated observations separate the two, and growth rates distinguish children with diagnosed speech and language difficulties better than single scores do [@dayModelingLongitudinalTrajectories2025]. This distinction -- level versus rate -- recurs throughout this report.

## Word learning in Down syndrome

Development differs from the very start: imaging shows differences in the size of several brain structures in newborns with Down syndrome, present before experience has had any chance to act [@fukami-gartnerComprehensiveVolumetricPhenotyping2023]. Children with Down syndrome generally learn words more slowly than typically developing children. They generally say fewer words than they understand, and they differ from one another considerably -- differences that increase over time [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020; @oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994; @berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @galeoteAcquisitionProductiveVocabulary2008; @kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013; @deckersPredictorsReceptiveExpressive2019].

First spoken words typically come later. Some children with Down syndrome begin at around the usual time; many do not say their first words until after 24 months. In one longitudinal study, children with Down syndrome learned their first 10 spoken words between 19 and 38 months of age [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994]; more than 80% of typically developing children reach this stage by 17 months [@frankWordbankOpenRepository2017].

The sections below take the machinery of word learning described above and ask where, for children with Down syndrome, it runs differently -- and what follows for teaching, and for the trajectories this study describes.

### Where learning is harder -- and where it is not

The mapping step itself appears comparatively robust. Matched for developmental level, children and young people with Down syndrome fast-map new object words about as well as typically developing children, inferring the link from context and understanding the word after brief exposure [@chapmanFastMappingWords1990]. Nor is retention necessarily the problem: small sets of newly taught words were retained over a full week by children with Down syndrome as well as by typically developing children [@sakhonSmallSetsNovel2018]. Understanding can be a genuine relative strength: infants with Down syndrome have been observed to understand *more* words than typically developing infants matched on nonverbal mental ability [@mason-appsInfantsSyndromeShow2020]. A larger Spanish study of 186 children with Down syndrome, each matched on mental age to a typically developing child, found the same for comprehension and for gesture, and read it as the dividend of experience: at any given mental age a child with Down syndrome is older, and has simply heard more [@galeoteDevelopmentVocabularySpanish2011]. The same fact shapes this report's comparisons -- where children with Down syndrome and typically developing children are compared at the same level of comprehension, the children with Down syndrome are the older group by the better part of a year (@sec-joint-outcomes).

The vulnerable component is the sound side of a word. Verbal short-term memory is disproportionately impaired in Down syndrome -- more than visuospatial memory, and more than overall development would predict [@naessLanguageVerbalShortterm2011]. On the classic account, this should severely constrain word learning [@baddeleyPhonologicalLoopLanguage1998]; in fact the constraint turns out to be specific. Verbal short-term memory relates to learning the *form* of new words, not to learning what they refer to -- and in Down syndrome, learning the form is impaired while learning the meaning is intact [@jarroldRelationshipsVerbalShortterm2009].

Meanwhile the slower, repetition-driven route appears largely preserved. Individuals with Down syndrome benefit from repetition of sound sequences as much as vocabulary-matched controls despite far smaller memory spans [@mosseSearchingHebbEffect2010], and across word-learning experiments they learned new words as well as vocabulary-matched controls -- better than their short-term memory alone would predict [@mosseEvidencePreservedNovel2011]. Word learning in Down syndrome appears to lean more heavily on cumulative, repetition-driven learning than typical development does.

Two further constraints bear on the same component. Fluctuating conductive hearing loss -- present in most children with Down syndrome in the early years (@sec-ds-hearing) -- degrades precisely the signal from which word forms must be built, blurring the differences between similar-sounding words ("cat", "hat", "mat"); children with Down syndrome who had hearing difficulties at ages 2 to 4 scored lower on vocabulary and language measures years later [@lawsEarlyHearingLoss2014]. Sleep is also often disrupted in young children with Down syndrome, and poorer sleep is associated with weaker expressive language development, consistent with a role for sleep-dependent consolidation [@edgin2015sleep].

Speech production carries the heaviest load of all. Differences in the anatomy of the mouth and vocal tract, lower muscle tone, and difficulty with the planning and coordination of speech movements all make spoken words harder to produce and harder for listeners to understand [@kentSpeechImpairmentSyndrome2013; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. Canonical babbling -- the repeated consonant–vowel syllables of "ba-ba" -- begins only a couple of months later than in typical development, but it is less stable once it has begun, and the move from babble to recognisable words takes far longer [@lynchOnsetSpeechlikeVocalizations1995; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. In the fast-mapping studies above, saying the new word was consistently the most fragile step: children with Down syndrome could infer and retain what a word meant well before they could produce it reliably [@chapmanFastMappingWords1990].

In short: the step that attaches meanings to words is relatively spared; the steps that encode a word's sound pattern and turn it into speech are not. This asymmetry organises much of what follows.

### Rates of word learning

Word learning accelerates rapidly for many typically developing children between the ages of 18 and 24 months. It is less clear whether, and when, children with Down syndrome experience a similar acceleration. Some studies observe one in some children and not others; where it occurs, it comes later than in typical development, though perhaps at a broadly similar developmental level [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994; @berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001; @zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. In a Dutch study that followed 26 toddlers month by month for 18 months from about 18 months of age, the children split roughly into thirds -- marginal growth, steady growth without a spurt, and growth with a spurt -- and the marginal-growth third had lower cognitive scores [@kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017]. If acceleration is what accumulating skill looks like, rather than a distinct event [@mcmurrayDefusingChildhoodVocabulary2007], then this is what slower accumulation should produce: a later, gentler rise, reached by different children at different ages -- not a missing "spurt" waiting to be triggered. The practical reading is to keep building the underlying system -- words heard, understood and practised -- rather than to wait for a step change.

### Words understood and words spoken

Whether spoken vocabulary lags behind words understood *disproportionately* -- beyond the lag seen in typical development -- is not settled. Estimates depend on how vocabulary is measured, whether gestures and signs are counted, the ages studied and how groups are compared [@martingklusekjestigarribiabjLanguageCharacteristicsIndividuals2009; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. One recent study benchmarked each group against the typical relation between words understood and words spoken: children with Williams syndrome sat above it, saying more of what they understood than typically developing children do, while 27 children with Down syndrome aged 12 to 39 months showed no such narrowing, and nor did 15 children with fragile X syndrome. Two thirds of the Down syndrome sample fell on the wider-gap side of that benchmark, though the study did not test that direction and the sample is small [@dsouzaExplainingComprehensionProduction2026].

The mechanisms above give the gap a natural reading. The steps that carry understanding are comparatively preserved, while the steps a spoken word needs -- an accurately stored sound pattern, then fluent articulation -- are exactly the impaired ones. A wide gap between what a child understands and what they say is, on this reading, an expected feature of vocabulary development in Down syndrome rather than, by itself, a cause for alarm -- and it means that spoken vocabulary alone will understate what a child knows. This is one reason this study models words understood and words spoken jointly, so that expectations for each can be read against the other (@sec-models).

### Words and the language built on them {#sec-ds-vocabulary-grammar}

Vocabulary is among the least affected parts of language in Down syndrome, and it is worth being precise about what that does and does not mean. Reviewing the profile component by component, @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020 place receptive vocabulary -- at least for concrete words -- at or above the level expected from nonverbal ability, spoken vocabulary generally below it, and expressive grammar furthest below: the ability to combine words into phrases and sentences, and to mark them with the small grammatical words and endings, lags even nonverbal mental age and is the component most severely affected [@chapmanLanguageSkillsChildren1998]. The vocabulary trajectories this report describes are therefore trajectories of the strongest language skill -- and of the one that the weaker skills are built from.

The link between words and grammar, however, is looser in Down syndrome than in typical development. In typically developing children grammar follows vocabulary closely, and the size of a child's spoken vocabulary is a good guide to when word combinations will begin [@batesInseparabilityGrammarLexicon1997]. In Down syndrome the guide still points the right way -- children with larger vocabularies combine words more -- but it runs late. Italian children with Down syndrome who produced as many single words as typically developing children of the same mental age nevertheless produced simpler, more telegraphic sentences and understood less grammar [@vicariAsynchronyLexicalMorphosyntactic2000]; at a matched vocabulary of several hundred words, children with Down syndrome combined words less often and produced few grammatically complete sentences [@zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011]; and longer utterances do not bring with them the verbs that longer utterances bring in typical development [@heskethVerbUseIndividuals1998]. A vocabulary large enough to support two-word phrases is therefore a signal that grammar can be taught, not a sign that it will follow on its own (@sec-intro).

Which words a child knows matters as well as how many. Several studies find that, relative to typically developing children at a similar level, children with Down syndrome use fewer verbs and fewer of the closed-class words -- articles, prepositions, pronouns -- that hold sentences together [@chapmanLanguageSkillsChildren1998; @zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011; @loveallVerbProductionIndividuals2019], though a Spanish study matched on vocabulary size found no difference in composition at all [@checaCompositionEarlyVocabulary2016], and children with Down syndrome understand what verbs mean well enough to use them to anticipate what comes next in a sentence, which suggests that the missing verbs are a grammatical problem more than a lexical one [@arias-trejoVerbmediatedAnticipatoryEye2019]. Whether teaching vocabulary, and verbs in particular, improves grammar is an open question [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. The counts this report models treat every word alike and cannot see this composition; that is a reason to read them as a measure of the foundation rather than of the language being built on it.

### Gestures and signs

Before and alongside speech, all children communicate with their hands. Pointing emerges towards the end of the first year, before first words, and words often appear in gesture before they appear in speech -- in children with Down syndrome as in typically developing children [@ozcaliskanEarlyGestureProvides2017]. How much a child conveys in gesture predicts the growth of their spoken vocabulary in typical development [@roweLearningWordsHand2008]. Gesture also anticipates grammar: the age at which a typically developing child first pairs a gesture with a word that says something different -- pointing at a bird while saying "nap" -- predicts the age at which two-word speech begins [@iversonGesturePavesWay2005].

Children with Down syndrome use this route more, and for longer. With spoken production constrained, gesture becomes a substantial channel of expression rather than a brief stepping stone: children with Down syndrome rely on gestures more than typically developing children at similar stages of vocabulary development, frequently conveying with a gesture a word they cannot yet say [@caselliGesturesWordsEarly1998; @stefaniniSpokenGesturalProduction2007]. A systematic review concluded that children with Down syndrome produce the same kinds of gestures and pass through the same early stages of expressive development as typically developing children, but later and over a longer period, and recommended deliberately incorporating gestures into everyday communication and early intervention [@tekaat-vandenosGesturesPaveWay2015]. The shift from gesture to speech is slow: in the Dutch monthly study above, most children stayed either mainly gestural or gestural-plus-spoken across the whole 18 months, and only four of the 26 moved from one profile to the next [@kaat-vandenosExpressiveVocabularyDevelopment2017].

The same route runs through Down syndrome, with two differences that bear on what comes next. The first is in communication before words. Infants and toddlers with Down syndrome respond to and initiate joint attention -- sharing attention to an object with another person -- about as well as typically developing children at the same developmental level, but they make fewer non-verbal requests [@mundyNonverbalCommunicationEarly1995; @fidlerNonverbalRequestingProblemsolving2005; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020], and requesting and commenting are the pre-verbal skills that best predict later language [@mundyNonverbalCommunicationEarly1995; @yoderEarlyPredictorsLanguage2004]. The second is in how gestures and words are combined. Children with Down syndrome pair a gesture with a word about as often as typically developing children at the same vocabulary size, but their pairings mostly say the same thing twice -- waving while saying "bye" -- whereas the pairings that predict two-word speech add a second element [@zampiniGestureProductionLanguage2011; @iversonGesturePavesWay2005]. Gesture and sign are therefore not only a route to words but a rehearsal for combining them. And a gesture is how a word is often asked for: parents of toddlers with Down syndrome put most of their children's gestures into words, and the things a parent has named in response to a gesture are the ones more likely to enter the child's own spoken vocabulary later [@dimitrovaParentsTranslationsChild2016].

Many families and practitioners do exactly that, teaching signs alongside spoken words. Signing fits the profile described above: it routes expression around the most impaired output system, leans on relatively stronger visual skills, and pairs a visible form with the spoken word without replacing it. In toddlers with Down syndrome, sign use predicts the size of later vocabulary [@ozcaliskanBabySignNot2016]. An implication for measurement follows: for young children with Down syndrome, expressive vocabulary is not a single spoken count. Several of the datasets pooled in this study record, word by word, whether a child signs it, says it or both, and the models treat signed production as an outcome in its own right (@sec-data, @sec-models).

### What this means for teaching and support {#sec-ds-teaching}

One further body of evidence belongs here, because it concerns the adults rather than the child. What parents do shapes vocabulary growth in every child, and it has been suggested that it matters more in Down syndrome, where a child has less capacity to make up for a thin environment [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. In toddlers with Down syndrome, the time a parent and child spend jointly engaged with the same object while the child attends to the words being used about it predicts later language over and above where the child started [@adamsonJointEngagementEmergence2009]. Mothers of infants and toddlers with Down syndrome work harder than mothers of typically developing children to hold their child's attention and to keep an object in play, and the children vocalise and communicate more when they do [@legersteeEffectsMaintainingRedirecting2002; @roachStructureMotherchildPlay1998]. The influence runs both ways, and not always helpfully: a child whose speech is hard to understand gives a parent less to expand on, and a child who persists less with objects gives a parent fewer gestures to put into words [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020]. The openings that word learning needs are therefore less likely to arise by themselves, and more likely to need engineering.

None of this amounts to a recipe, but the mechanisms converge on principles that fit both how words are learned and where, in Down syndrome, learning is constrained and where it is not.

- **Protect the input.** Word learning runs on hearing, and in Down syndrome the input is often degraded exactly when learning is most intensive. Active surveillance and management of hearing, and attention to background noise and speaking distance, protect the signal. Vision matters too: many young children with Down syndrome focus poorly on near objects even when wearing glasses [@creggAccommodationRefractiveError2001] -- and the pictures, books and signs through which much teaching happens are near objects.
- **Name what the child is attending to.** The best word-learning moments are ones in which the object is already at the centre of the child's attention [@pereiraBottomupViewToddler2014; @yuInfantSustainedAttention2019], and in Down syndrome it is this joint engagement that predicts later language [@adamsonJointEngagementEmergence2009]. Following the child's focus and naming it beats redirecting them -- though holding a child's attention in the first place may take more work than it does with other children [@legersteeEffectsMaintainingRedirecting2002; @roachStructureMotherchildPlay1998].
- **Put the child's gestures into words.** A gesture or a sign is usually a bid for a word. Parents of toddlers with Down syndrome already translate most of their children's gestures into speech, and the things a parent has named in reply to a gesture are the ones more likely to enter the child's own vocabulary [@dimitrovaParentsTranslationsChild2016]. When the child pairs a gesture or sign with a word, reply with the two-word phrase it implies.
- **Provide many, spaced encounters, and expect learning to be cumulative.** Repeating a new word within an episode helps, and so does returning to it across days [@schwabRepetitionSuccessiveSentences2016; @benjaminWhatMakesDistributed2010]. Varied examples -- the same word across different objects, pictures and settings -- support generalisation [@vukatanaOneNotEnough2015]. Distributed repetition is precisely the structure the preserved, cumulative route in Down syndrome needs; one-off exposure taxes exactly the impaired short-term route [@mosseEvidencePreservedNovel2011].
- **Teach understanding ahead of speech, and count more than spoken words.** Comprehension can run well ahead of production, and building it is the foundation production draws on. Signs and gestures let a child express words they cannot yet say [@ozcaliskanBabySignNot2016], and written words offer a further visual route into language [@burgoyneEfficacyReadingLanguage2012].
- **Give saying words explicit, sustained practice.** Production is the most fragile component and the slowest to consolidate [@chapmanFastMappingWords1990; @kentSpeechImpairmentSyndrome2013]. Opportunities to say words -- and to be understood -- need to be engineered, not just hoped for.
- **Do not wait for grammar to follow.** In typical development, word combinations follow vocabulary closely; in Down syndrome they lag behind it, and the words grammar most needs -- verbs and the small function words -- are the ones children with Down syndrome are least likely to have (@sec-ds-vocabulary-grammar). Grammar can be taught [@sepulvedaCanIndividualsSyndrome2013], and a vocabulary large enough for two-word phrases is the cue to start.
- **Do not read memory test scores as a ceiling.** Poor performance on memory span or repetition tasks indexes one route into vocabulary, not a child's capacity to learn words [@mosseEvidencePreservedNovel2011].

## From word learning to trajectories

These principles say something about how to teach words. They say little about what to expect: how many words, understood or spoken, at which ages, with what spread. Yet expectations are where practice most often goes wrong. An expectation borrowed from typical development will reliably be missed, while "children with Down syndrome are delayed" is too vague to guide anything.

What families and practitioners need is the distribution itself: the trajectories of words understood, signed and spoken among children with Down syndrome, the ranges within which most children travel, and the ages at which milestones are typically reached. Against these, an individual child's vocabulary becomes interpretable. Typical progress for this population can be recognised as such, and a child travelling unusually slowly even against these expectations can be identified early and investigated rather than absorbed into a general expectation of delay.

Hearing comes first (@sec-ds-hearing), but it is not the only thing to check. Congenital heart disease serious enough to need surgery in the first year, thyroid disorder, a history of infantile spasms, disrupted sleep and autism all occur more often in Down syndrome than in the general population, and each has been associated with poorer language [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020; @edgin2015sleep] -- early heart surgery, for instance, with lower receptive and expressive language scores as a toddler, though not by school age [@alsaiedCongenitalHeartDisease2016]. A child whose vocabulary sits well below the expectations described here is a child in whom these are worth ruling out.

Because level and rate are different facts, repeated observations that locate a trajectory tell more than any single count [@dayModelingLongitudinalTrajectories2025]. A large pool of observations also bears on a question that single studies have not settled. One longitudinal study reported children with Down syndrome acquiring much the same early vocabulary as typically developing children, a year to eighteen months later, with the gap widening as development went on [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994]; whether the trajectory is the typical curve shifted later and stretched, or a differently shaped curve, remains open [@abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020], and the contrast with typically developing children that this study draws (@sec-intro) speaks to it directly. Estimating these trajectories and ranges accurately, from a far larger pool of observations than any single study can provide, is the purpose of this study (@sec-intro); the data and models that follow (@sec-data, @sec-models) are built to that end.
